newsitem.title: USA: Fight over NYC rent controls bogs down over blame.
newsitem.headline: Fight over NYC rent controls bogs down over blame.

text.p: A heated fight in New York State over apartment rent rules that has stymied the state's budget bogged down over who was to blame for the impasse, with the Assembly Speaker pinning the blame on Gov George Pataki.

"The only person responsible for ensuring that you keep your homes, that you get to stay in neighborhoods you resurrected, that middle class families remain a vital part of this city is the governor," said Assembly Speaker Sheldon Silver, D-Manhattan, according to a copy of his speech.
Saying voters should remember Pataki's silence on election day, Silver added: "What kind of government intentionally scares millions of families with the threat of taking away their homes?"

The Democrat addressed about 100 voters from the Bronx and Riverdale, who traveled by bus to Albany, according to Assemblyman Jeff Dinowitz, D-Bronx. He said the rally was an outgrowth of town meetings he has held, adding it also was sponsored by Assemblyman Jeffrey Klein, D-Bronx, New York Senator Franz Leichter, D-Manhattan, and New York City Councilwoman June Eisland of the Bronx.
A spokesman for the Republican governor responded to Silver's charge by pointing to criticism of the Democrat lawmaker that was voiced by former New York City Mayor Ed Koch.
"Anyone who needs to understand the problem with rent control should reference Mayor Koch's comments in the media today," said Mike McKeon, a Pataki spokesman.
The New York Post on Tuesday quoted Koch as saying: "The person who is most responsible for frightening people is Shelly Silver...by saying he doesn't want any changes."
The Assembly has approved a bill that would make permanent the present rent rules, which mainly affect New York City as it has the lion's share of the state's regulated apartments.

But Senate Majority Leader Joseph Bruno, R-Troy, who has threatened to let the rules expire on June 15, only wants to keep protections for the elderly, the needy and the disabled, though he has said he would consider phasing the rules out over four years instead of two as he first proposed.

The governor, who wants to mediate the dispute, previously has said he favored vacancy decontrol, but the Assembly opposes this policy. It says an experiment with vacany decontrol in the mid-1970s led some landlords to harass tenants so that they would quit their apartments, allowing free-market rents to be charged.
The New York Post said Koch had gotten Bruno to endorse a plan for vacancy decontrol and a reduction in the $250,000 earning level that also returns apartments to the free market system.
